title: Cervix Anatomy: Transformation Zone, Canal & Epithelium
description: Understand cervix anatomy at the lower uterus, comparing the mucus-secreting endocervical canal, squamous ectocervix, internal and external os, and stroma.
h1: Cervix Anatomy: Endocervix, Ectocervix and Transformation Zone
blurb: The collagen-dense lower neck of the uterus, where mucus-secreting columnar endocervical epithelium meets squamous ectocervix at the transformation zone.
lead: Acting as the structural gatekeeper between the vaginal canal and uterine cavity, the cervix combines a collagen-dense wall with a dynamic epithelial junction. In this illustrated guide to cervix anatomy and transformation zone, we examine 20 documented structures—including ectocervix, endocervical canal, endocervical columnar epithelium, ectocervical squamous epithelium—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Acting as the structural gatekeeper between the vaginal canal and uterine cavity, the cervix combines a collagen-dense wall with a dynamic epithelial junction. Learn which epithelium lines each surface and why the transformation zone matters for cervical cytology and colposcopy — without turning anatomy into a screening guideline. Within the human body, the cervix — transformation zone (Cervix uteri) is situated in uterine neck projecting into vaginal fornices, receives arterial perfusion via descending uterine + vaginal branches, and is innervated by uterovaginal plexus; pelvic visceral afferents.

Structurally, the ectocervix (Portio vaginalis cervicis) comprises part of cervix visible at the vaginal vault. Physiologically, the ectocervix governs covered by nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium. Structurally, the endocervical canal (Canalis cervicis uteri) comprises canal linking internal to external os. Physiologically, the endocervical canal conducts sperm and menstrual flow; glandular mucus changes cyclically. Structurally, the endocervical columnar epithelium (Epithelium columnare) comprises mucus-secreting simple columnar lining of the canal. Physiologically, the endocervical columnar epithelium produces cervical mucus under hormonal regulation. Structurally, the ectocervical squamous epithelium (Epithelium squamosum) comprises nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium continuous with vaginal mucosa. Physiologically, the ectocervical squamous epithelium protects exposed cervical surface. Structurally, the squamocolumnar junction (Junctio squamocolumnaris) comprises border where glandular and squamous epithelia meet. Physiologically, the squamocolumnar junction governs migrates with age, hormones and pregnancy. Structurally, the transformation zone (Zona transformationis) comprises region of squamous metaplasia between original and current SCJ. Physiologically, the transformation zone governs physiologic remodeling of exposed columnar epithelium.

Clinically, regarding the ectocervix, visual examination and directed biopsy sample this surface. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the endocervical canal, stenosis may obstruct sampling or menstrual outflow. In clinical pathology involving the endocervical columnar epithelium, glandular lesions need distinct cytologic evaluation. Medical evaluation of the ectocervical squamous epithelium also notes that squamous metaplasia alters the visible junction.

questions.question: What is the cervical transformation zone?
questions.answer: It is the region where squamous epithelium of the ectocervix and columnar epithelium of the endocervix meet and change over time.

questions.question: Why is the transformation zone important in cervical screening?
questions.answer: Many cervical precancerous changes arise near the squamocolumnar junction. Screening samples this region, but this atlas does not interpret individual test results.

questions.question: What is the ectocervix?
questions.answer: The ectocervix is the portion of the cervix that projects into the vagina and is visible during a speculum examination.

questions.question: Where is the endocervical columnar epithelium located?
questions.answer: Simple columnar epithelium lines the endocervical canal and secretes mucus.

questions.question: What is the squamocolumnar junction, and how does it change?
questions.answer: It is the boundary between glandular columnar and squamous epithelia; its position shifts with age, hormones and pregnancy.
